articles.title: Patrick Stewart's Secret Comedy Roles Deserve To Be Part of His Legacy Alongside Star Trek & X-Men
articles.summary: Patrick Stewart’s legacy is largely tied to his role as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men, with his last acting appearance premiering in December with Avengers: Doomsday. His voice is distinct, standing out among his peers, and casual viewers no doubt associate the actor with seriousness. However, for Stewart’s whole […]
articles.content:
However, for Stewart’s whole career, he had wanted to do comedy. He was rarely cast in comedy roles. During his career with the Royal Shakespeare Company, he was cast as Touchstone, the fool of Duke Frederick, for the 1968 production of As You Like It. Touchstone is typically a comedy role, given that he’s a jester. The director for As You Like It had a different take on the character, however, envisioning him as a sad, old man. It was that version of the character that the director felt Stewart would be perfect for.

Still, through collaborations with Seth MacFarlane , known for the television shows Family Guy and American Dad , and Ricky Gervais, audiences saw another side of Patrick Stewart — a comedic one. Stewart’s wit could be used for humor, and although the roles were never quite as popular as Picard and Xavier, they deserve to be part of Patrick Stewart’s legacy.

Patrick Stewart often credited Seth MacFarlane with having the greatest impact on his career regarding comedy. MacFarlane helped people see that there was another actor inside Patrick Stewart. Since his days at the Royal Shakespeare Company, other actors loved saying lines in Stewart’s voice, finding amusement, but they didn’t find Stewart himself funny.

Stewart had recurring voice roles in MacFarlane projects such as Family Guy and American Dad. For American Dad , Stewart voiced the inner thoughts of Baby Susie Swanson. Baby Susie was too young to speak, with her dialogue on the show mainly being noises voiced by Christina Milian. However, the show sometimes highlighted her inner thoughts. Not only were they in Patrick Stewart’s voice, but Stewart broke the fourth wall, directly asking the audience, “How are you liking the program so far?” In American Dad , Stewart wasn’t working against his voice, but rather it was working for him. It’s funny to think about a little girl’s thoughts coming out in the voice of Patrick Stewart, and to think that even a shred of Stewart’s consciousness doesn’t mind being trapped in said brain.

Additionally, Stewart acted in the sitcom Blunt Talk , which aired for two seasons between 2015 and 2016 and was executive produced by McFarlane. Blunt Talk featured Stewart as Walter Blunt — who shared the name of Stewart’s first role with the Royal Shakespeare Company, Sir Walter Blunt of Henry IV, Part I — who was a British newscaster who moved to LA. Blunt’s main ambition through the series was to conquer American nightly news, but he quickly found out that his goal was harder to achieve than initially thought.

Blunt Talk was met with mixed reviews from critics, with many believing the show mistook being vulgar for being witty in its comedy. Still, it was undeniable that Blunt Talk positioned Stewart as he hadn’t been before. Blunt Talk’s home network of Starz allowed the show to go to extreme places audiences hadn’t quite associated Stewart with, whether it was struggling in an airport men’s stall or in vulgar sexual encounters. Even if the show might not have been good, it’s worth checking out for Stewart’s performance.

In 2005, Patrick Stewart guest-starred in an episode of Ricky Gervais’s Extras. Stewart had been a fan of Gervais’s since The Office , finding the show genius, and couldn’t believe what he was hearing when Gervais called. Apparently, Stewart had a friend who loved doing impressions of famous people on the phone, so Stewart had assumed it wasn’t Gervais calling.

For Extras , Stewart played an exaggerated version of himself alongside Gervais’s role of a young actor still starting out who was cast as an extra in a production. Stewart gives him advice, emphasizing the impact of writing your own screenplay, and is very candid when Gervais asks about it. Taking inspiration from his character Charles Xavier in X-Men , Stewart’s exaggerated self wrote a screenplay about what it’d be like to have telepathy and telekinesis in the real world, one without superheroes. Stewart reveals that his character in the script is obsessed with undressing women. The episode plays the character’s stonefaced seriousness around being a perv for comedy, with even Gervais assuming Stewart must be joking.

In Patrick Stewart: A Knight of Comedy , Stewart delivered his own eulogy, which quickly devolved into a tale of previous sexual exploits. What starts with Stewart talking big about himself — calling himself “the greatest actor ever” — turns into stories throughout his life of having sex with inanimate objects, including the variety of props at the RSC.

Which Patrick Stewart comedy role made you laugh the hardest? Let us know in the comments below!

articles.title: Franco-Moroccan Director Nabil Ayouch on Exploring ‘More Intimacy in My Characters’ With Next Film ‘Run, With No Tears’
articles.summary: For Franco-Moroccan filmmaker Nabil Ayouch, the freedom to tell the stories in which he believes has always mattered more than winning universal approval. Over nearly three decades, he has built a career exploring complex social realities and giving a voice to characters determined to challenge the limits imposed upon their lives. Along the way, he […]
articles.content:
For Franco-Moroccan filmmaker Nabil Ayouch , the freedom to tell the stories in which he believes has always mattered more than winning universal approval. Over nearly three decades, he has built a career exploring complex social realities and giving a voice to characters determined to challenge the limits imposed upon their lives. Along the way, he has learned to embrace the possibility that his films won't always be understood.

"Making films means taking the risk of being misunderstood," Ayouch tells Variety at the 47th Cairo Intl. Film Festival, where he serves as president of the international competition jury and was honored with the Golden Pyramid Lifetime Achievement Award at the festival's opening ceremony. "Everyone wants to be loved. But if all I wanted was to be loved, I think I'd do something other than cinema." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'Cher Adores Michael Douglas,' Icon's Rep Says After Douglas Disses Her Oscar Win for 'Moonstruck' Hollywood Still Faces Weekend Disruptions After FAA Lifts Flight Ground Stop

"It's more important for me to express myself, to say what I have to say, to try to be understood, to touch souls, than to be loved," he adds.

His return to Cairo carries particular significance. Nearly three decades ago, Ayouch presented his debut feature, "Mektoub," at the festival, where it won two awards. Since then, he has returned several times, drawn to a city whose energy he describes as both overwhelming and exhilarating.

But the convictions that first drove Ayouch to make films remain as strong as ever. "The rage that has driven me since I started making cinema is intact, perhaps even stronger today," he reflects, pointing to the injustices he sees around the world. "Every morning, I wake up full of this energy, this anger, but also full of love and passion for human beings. I want to continue seeing the beauty of this world and telling it through films." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

That tension between anger and hope has its roots in Ayouch's childhood in Sarcelles, a working-class suburb north of Paris, where he spent his formative years. He credits the teachers and youth workers at a local youth and cultural center with helping him channel difficult experiences into something constructive.

"They taught me how to transform things that hurt me and that rage into a saving energy," he recalls. "I don't think I would have become a director" without them.

The experience has shaped not only his filmmaking but also his efforts to support emerging talent. Ayouch has opened seven cultural centers across Morocco, hoping to offer young people opportunities similar to those that changed his own life.

His films, from "Ali Zaoua" and "Casablanca Beats" to "Much Loved" and "Everybody Loves Touda," have consistently focused on people seeking to take control of their own lives. But Ayouch resists defining his characters solely through their suffering.

"I need to meet someone whose soul attracts me, not simply because they've had a difficult life, but because of their desire to escape a cage, to break free from something that confines them," he says. "I don't like characters who are victims."

Ayouch believes his refusal to portray women as powerless was a key reason "Much Loved," his 2015 drama about sex workers in Marrakech, sparked such controversy in Morocco.

"Things would have been much simpler if the women in the film had been poor women who were beaten from beginning to end," he says. "It's because they're seeking independence, because they're demanding and want to escape their circumstances, that the film caused so much trouble."

The controversy surrounding "Much Loved" prompted moments of doubt, but Ayouch insists that provoking outrage has never been his objective.

"I don't make films to create controversy," he maintains. "I make films because something outrages me, and I can't imagine that those films won't be divisive."

Ayouch is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and France's Académie des Césars. As president of Cairo's international competition jury, he prefers to enter screenings knowing as little as possible about the filmmakers or their stories. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"I like to be surprised," he says. "Cinema is an encounter, a shock, a moment of wonder." He is particularly drawn to films that continue to reveal themselves long after the credits roll.

When it comes to jury deliberations, he favors discussion and consensus over voting, hoping that the jury's diverse perspectives will help them reach a collective decision rather than one imposed by majority rule.

Despite receiving a lifetime achievement award, Ayouch is hardly ready to call it a day. He jokingly dubbed it a "mid-lifetime achievement award," making clear that he hopes to have plenty more films ahead of him.

Looking ahead, he is interested in a different approach. "I'd like to explore a little more intimacy in my characters," he reveals. "To make cinema that's less political, and to find politics elsewhere, particularly in intimacy."

That exploration will continue with his next feature, "Run, With No Tears," which is scheduled to begin shooting in Morocco in early January. The film will star Vimala Pons, who replaces the previously announced Noomi Rapace, alongside Maryam Touzani and Nisrin Erradi, reuniting Ayouch with two actresses from his previous work. The film will be produced via his company Ali n' Productions.

While he is eager to explore new directions, Ayouch has little interest in revisiting or correcting his earlier work. "If I had to remake the films I've made, I'd remake them all, scene by scene, film by film, and change absolutely nothing."

articles.title: Anthony Mackie Defends His Viral Comments About Vision And Doomsday (But Do We Believe Him?)
articles.summary: So is Paul Bettany actually in Doomsday?
articles.content:
It's an exciting time to be a Marvel fans, given the release of VisionQuest' s finale for those with a Disney+ subscription , as well as the upcoming Marvel movie Avengers: Doomsday being a month and change away from its release. Just last week, Anthony Mackie went viral for seemingly spoiling Paul Bettany's role in Doomsday , but now he's defending those comments. The question is: do we actually believe him?

This potentially offers some much-needed context about Mackie's viral comments about hanging out with Paul Bettany while shooting Doomsday . If the actor is to be believed, he knew that VisionQuest was also shooting at Pinewood Studios in the U.K. at the same time as principal photography for the next Avengers flick. That's how he was able to see his frequent co-star, instead of shooting the crossover event together.

The "I guess" certainly doesn't inspire confidence. Given Marvel's tight security , actors sometimes have to tell white lies in order to guard the shared universe's spoilers. Case in point: Andrew Garifeld lied about returning as Spider-Man for years ahead of No Way Home 's release. As such, we're going to have to wait until the next Avengers movie hits theaters to find out whether or not Mackie was telling the truth about Bettany (and Holland).

articles.title: Golshifteh Farahani and Director Chabname Zariab on Anti-Taliban Film ‘When She Hears the Bells,’ Sold by Le Pacte
articles.summary: TALLINN, Estonia — The striking images of Kabul international airport stormed by thousands of Afghans and foreigners desperately trying to be evacuated by U.S. planes as Kabul fell into the hands of the Taliban, have stayed etched in many people’s minds. For Afghan-born Paris-based writer and director Chabname Zariad, long-listed for an Oscar with her […]
articles.content:
TALLINN, Estonia — The striking images of Kabul international airport stormed by thousands of Afghans and foreigners desperately trying to be evacuated by U.S. planes as Kabul fell into the hands of the Taliban, have stayed etched in many people's minds.

For Afghan-born Paris-based writer and director Chabname Zariad, long-listed for an Oscar with her short film "Hizia," the takeover of Afghanistan from the hard-line Islamist group, was a gut-wrenching experience that immediately triggered her desire to spotlight in a movie their authoritarian regime and especially crackdown on women. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss Reunite at Travis Kelce’s Chiefs Game Against Jets Taylor Swift to Perform at CMAs for the First Time in 13 Years

That film -"When She Hears the Bells" ("Les clochettes de Kaboul”) is now an intense thriller drama shepherded by France's Alta Rocca Films and repped by Le Pacte , with star-actress Goldshifteh Farahani ("Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales," "Alpha") in the title role. Co-producing partners take in Belgium's Versus Production, Germany's Starhaus Filmproduktion and Arte France Cinéma. Both Zariab and Farahani are in Tallinn for the film's world premiere on Nov. 18 at the Black Nights Film Festival's first feature competition .

The film, penned by the filmmaker with her sister Parande Zariab, is set in the Summer of 2021, as Kabul is on the verge of falling into the hands of the Taliban. We follow the young widow Leila (Farahani), who arrives in Kabul and starts working in a kitchen, set in a "Bacha Bazi" house.

The term (literally meaning playing with boys in Persian) refers to a controversial yet still practiced tradition in Central Asia, "particularly in conservative and religious countries," notes Zariab, whereby young boys, dressed as women, are forced to dance in front of men, and are subject to all kind of abuses. In the film, Leila decides to help a group of Bacha Bazi boys flee their horrendous fate, as Kabul edges closer to collapse. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Speaking with Variety on the near eve of the film's world premiere, the director says she returned to the topic of the Bacha Bazi – depicted in her 2015 short film "When You Hear the Bells" – not to further dig into the subject but to use it as a symbol of the state of a complex society under Taliban rule. "In reality, when you remove women from the public sphere, you also repress the desire for them which leaves room for all types of abuses. It becomes a sick society," she notes.

To raise awareness on the topic and attract the largest audience possible, Zariab and her sister borrowed from genre codes. The helmer who referenced Tarik Saleh's films and Saeed Roustayi's Cannes-selected "Leila's Brothers," said once she had built the form, the substance fell into place.

Hiring French-based Iranian actress Farahani for the title role was "an obvious choice."

"Ever since I had seen Golshifteh in Asghar Farhadi's "About Elly, " I had followed her career and in Atiq Rahimi's "The Patience Stone," she spoke an impeccable authentic Afghan Persian. Then her activism for women's rights also played a major part for me. Not only did she deliver an exceptional performance, but her professionalism on set was astonishing," says the helmer who cast her against mostly Afghan theatre actors and non-professionals to keep it authentic.

Farahani on Her Motivation Sharing with Variety why she boarded the project, Farahani says: "First of course, it was the powerful, well-written script and the humanitarian message behind it. The story needed to be told. Second, it was the incredible perseverance of Chabname who never gave up on me. And finally, it was that inner feeling telling me there was no way I could skip this one. As if it were simply part of what was written."

About her character Leila, the actress, who was bestowed Locarno Festival's prestigious Excellence Award, Davide Campari in 2025 , says she was compelled by "her ability to adapt and change. It reflects something you see so much in this region: how most people specially women can evolve in ways you might never imagine when they are forced to survive.

“It also reveals the potential within every human being to be pushed to the edge and find absolute courage, driven by dignity and human values. From a frightened, lonely woman to a lioness who decides to change the destiny of these [Bacha Bazi] children, even at the risk of her own life." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Farahani says working with children and first-time actors was both a challenge and a blessing in disguise. "When it works at its best, it becomes one of the most pleasant and rewarding parts of the job. They can become the most wonderful acting partners," she says, citing in particular the impeccable performance from Fatima Tawakkuli who plays Leila's co-worker and friend Mari, and newcomer Mojtaba Ahmadi, aka the elder Basha Bazi dancer Tamin.

Zariab says the initial plan was to shoot in Iraqi Kurdistan which bears resemblance to Afghanistan, but when bombing between Israel and Iran started in 2024, the movie eventually rolled in Morocco. To capture wide shots of Kabul, she asked a friend cinematographer in Afghanistan to fill in.

For her feature debut, the helmer is grateful for the support she got from her entire team, especially Farahani, cinematographer Pierre Cottereau ("Café de Flore"), and her first AD Benjamin Blanc.

On the production front, she cites French producers Lou Chicoteaux and Jean-Etienne Brat of Alta Rocca Films (behind her 2020 short “Hizia"), Arte Cinéma and Le Pacte –~in charge of sales and French distribution – as "truly exceptional partners who understood the urgency of this film and the significance of its subject matter." "I'm well aware that I was fortunate to have such a substantial budget [€3.5 million or $3.8 million) for my debut, especially at a time when funding is tightening across the board," concedes Zariab.

Chicoteaux and Brat also admit that "getting people on board this wild adventure" was not an easy ride. "Yet we had a director whose legitimacy was beyond question as she herself had fled her home country because of the Taliban. From the West, she watched her nation suffer and sink into despair and had to make this film," Brat explains.

Ultimately for him, "beyond the Bacha Bazi phenomenon which serves as potent symbol for the deviations that can emerge in societies undergoing intense radicalisation," "When She Hears the Bells "is at its core "the story of a woman who risks her own life to save children; She emerges as a true heroine." Commenting on the pic's resistance statement, Farahani adds: "Artists tell stories about these horrors and make people pay attention to what is happening in our world. Kino Lorber has picked up U.S. distribution rights to Edward Said: Between Worlds , Maiken Baird's archival documentary on the influential Palestinian scholar and activist. Kino Lorber is planning a 2027 theatrical release for the film.

Baird, an executive producer of projects like Bryan Fogel's Oscar-winning Icarus (2017) and Orwell: 2+2=5 (2025) from Raoul Paul, drew on extensive archive footage, including home movies, rare television appearances and public debates, to trace the evolution of Said's thought and his political awakening. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV 'Slow Horses' Lands Early Renewal for Seasons 9 and 10 at Apple TV Movies Gerard Depardieu Drops Appeal Against Sexual Assault Conviction, Admits Guilt

The documentary, made in collaboration with the Said family and his estate , spans seven decades from Said's childhood in Jerusalem to his migration, first to Egypt during the 1948 Palestine war, and finally to the United States, where Said became a noted academic in comparative literature at Columbia University. A prominent academic and cultural critic, Said was among the founders of the field of post-colonial studies. His 1978 book Orientalism, which critiqued Western cultural representations of the Eastern world, was a foundational text. The film also tracks Said's work as an activist, including his long-time advocacy for a Palestinian state, and his extensive efforts in the media to explain Palestinian history to a Western public.

“Shortly after October 7th, I found myself missing Edward Said – his voice, humanity and his remarkable powers of speech on Palestinian history and struggle for self-determination,” Baird sasid in a statement. “This film is both a reminder of Edward Said's brilliance and an introduction for a new generation who care deeply about the necessity of Palestinian rights.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });
